**Finding: deviation (high severity) — one redline to § 2.1.**

The termination architecture itself is fine. § 9.4 already tracks our preferred position almost word-for-word: Customer convenience termination of the Agreement or any Order Form on thirty days' notice, in whole or in part, refund of prepaid Fees allocable to the post-termination period, and an express statement that Vendor has no corresponding convenience right during a committed term. I searched the full document and found no Vendor convenience right anywhere, and § 9.5 confirms termination rights are non-exclusive and that terminating one Order Form doesn't cascade. § 27.3 adds a separate penalty-free force-majeure exit. Nothing to fix in Article 9.

The problem is § 2.1, which the planner flagged. It locks Customer into a three-year, USD 2,000,000-per-year take-or-pay minimum "without reduction or termination rights." Two things make this serious:

1. **No order-of-precedence clause exists** in the agreement — I searched for one specifically. So § 2.1, as the more specific commitment, can be argued to override the general convenience right in § 9.4.
2. **Even if § 9.4 survives**, Customer walks away and still owes the entire unpaid minimum. The exit cost reaches up to three years of committed spend, which dwarfs the fallback ceiling of three months' fees and puts us in walk-away territory: a multi-year term with no economically real convenience right.

So the right target was § 2.1, not § 9.4 — editing the termination clause would have accomplished nothing while the commitment language stood. The redline keeps Copperleaf's commercial minimum intact but carves terminations out of it, so the commitment reduces pro rata and no shortfall or early-termination amount is triggered by an exit under § 9.4 or any other provision.

One point worth flagging for the negotiation: I drafted this at the preferred level (no exit fee at all). If Copperleaf pushes back on losing all recovery against a $6M commitment, the playbook fallback supports an early-termination fee capped at three months' fees, and I noted that opening in the comment rather than conceding it up front.
